pools.name: US banks' and credit unions' spend on core, digital-banking and processing vendors (Fiserv, FIS, Jack Henry)
pools.size_basis: Sum of segment revenues: Fiserv Financial Solutions FY2025 $9,664M; FIS Banking Solutions FY2025 $7,285M; Jack Henry FY2026 about $2.55B (my derivation: 10-K says revenue rose 7.1% or $169M). Ceiling for US bank/CU spend since it includes some non-US and card-issuer processing revenue; other vendors (nCino, Q2, Alkami) not counted. US share not verified.
pools.money_flow: About 4,400 banks and 4,300 credit unions (rounded, from memory) pay the big three multi-year per-account and per-transaction fees for core ledgers, digital banking, card/payments processing and ancillary software, with termination and deconversion fees on exit.
pools.shock: Fiserv stock fell about 44-48% after its Oct 2025 miss and guidance reset; Q2-2026 (reported 2026-08-06): banking organic revenue -10%, total revenue -3%, 2026 guide cut to -1% to flat organic and EPS $7.20-7.40, head of Financial Solutions resigned in July 2026, product mix under review. At the same time bank M&A approvals fell to about 4 months (shortest since 1990), the FDIC proposed easing merger review in Sept 2026, and Q4-25/Q1-26 deal value hit multi-year highs. Every merger forces a core/data conversion.
pools.incumbents: Fiserv (about a third of community-bank cores per one analyst), FIS, Jack Henry. They capture money through 5-10 year contracts, deconversion fees and decades of lock-in.
pools.incumbent_fragility: Fiserv is distracted (guidance reset, executive departures, product review) and its DNA core is reportedly the most disliked and least likely to be renewed (consultant survey, secondary). Counter: management says attrition is stable and core contracts run for decades, so churn will be slow. Fragility is real but a decade-scale migration, not a sudden break.
pools.funded_startups_already_here: Core/BaaS layer (named from memory, funding years not re-verified this session): Nymbus, Thought Machine, 10x Banking, Mambu, Narmi; Finxact was bought by Fiserv in 2022; public peers nCino, Q2, Alkami. Services/middleware layer (conversion, contract benchmarking): none found, but no dedicated funding search was run.
pools.wedge_hints: (1) Core-contract benchmarking and renegotiation for $1-10B banks and CUs on a savings success fee. (2) Merger-conversion toolkits (data mapping, deconversion, parallel testing, vendor-exit project management) sold to the acquirer, a named buyer with a deal-driven budget. (3) Real-time data/API layer over legacy cores so banks can add products without a core swap. (4) Third-party risk management for bank-vendor oversight.
pools.insider_roles: COOs/CIOs of $1-10B community banks; core-conversion project managers; bank M&A integration officers; vendor-contract negotiators at bank consultancies; credit union CEOs; former core-vendor account managers.

pools.name: US mortgage servicers' operating cost (call centers, escrow, collections, loss mitigation, foreclosure, systems)
pools.size_basis: My derivation from MBA Servicing Operations Study: fully loaded cost 2024 was $176 per performing loan and $1,573 per non-performing loan. Assumed 50-55M first-lien loans (NOT verified; consistent with Valon's claim that 1 in 6 US mortgages is under contract to it): about 52M x $176 = $9.2B plus about 2.6M loans 30+ days late or in foreclosure (4.37% + 0.67%) x $1,573 = $4.1B. Range $11-14B. MBA's 2025 direct cost is $185 per loan, about 75% of it non-default.
pools.money_flow: Investors/MSR owners (Fannie, Freddie, Ginnie, banks, non-banks) pay servicers via the servicing-fee strip; servicers spend it on operations. The operating cost is the addressable pool.
pools.shock: Pandemic-era FHA loss-mitigation options expired end of Sept 2025 and trial payment plans keep loans delinquent until a permanent workout. MBA Q2-2026: total delinquency 4.37% (+44 bps YoY), FHA 11.79% (+122 bps YoY), VA 4.89%, foreclosure inventory 0.67% (+19 bps); FHA foreclosure inventory highest since Q4-2018, VA highest since Q2-2017; VA partial-claim program still awaiting guidance. Default cost is about 9x performing cost, so delinquency growth moves the pool fast.
pools.incumbents: Platforms: ICE Mortgage Technology (MSP; expanded Wells Fargo servicing deal) and Sagent. Servicers: large non-banks (Rithm/Newrez, Carrington, ServiceMac) and banks, running on decades-old systems plus offshore call centers.
pools.incumbent_fragility: Agency rules (FHA loss mitigation, VA, Ginnie) change faster than legacy vendors ship, and cost per loan keeps rising (systems $36, customer service $33 per loan in the MBA 2025 breakdown). Valon claims over $200M contracted ARR from servicers covering 1 in 6 US mortgages, so the legacy lock is cracking, though large migrations (Newrez) start only in 2027.
pools.funded_startups_already_here: Valon: $150M Series D at $2.3B valuation on 2026-10-05 (Ribbit, a16z); earlier $50M Series A (2021) and $100M Series C (2024); sold its own servicing ops to Carrington in 2026 and now sells ValonOS plus AI agents (customers Newrez, Carrington, ServiceMac). Competitors are incumbents ICE and Sagent. No funded startup found focused specifically on FHA/VA default operations.
pools.wedge_hints: FHA/VA default operations: loss-mitigation packet assembly, trial-payment-plan tracking, partial-claim processing, and avoiding Ginnie/FHA curtailments (investor penalties for late or wrong claims); subservicing for small non-bank servicers; REO/property preservation and foreclosure-timeline management; escrow/insurance-shortfall handling as homeowner premiums climb; priced per resolution or per loan below the $1,573 default cost.
pools.insider_roles: Heads of default servicing at subservicers; loss-mitigation negotiators; FHA/Ginnie compliance officers; MSR traders; property-preservation vendor owners; foreclosure attorneys.

pools.name: US title insurance premiums and settlement fees paid by home buyers and refinancers
pools.size_basis: ALTA 2025 full-year: $18.5B premiums written, +13.8% vs 2024; net income $1.168B; claims paid $667M. Q2-2026 premiums $5.3B vs $4.5B in Q2-2025. Settlement/escrow fees come on top and are not counted. Agents keep most of the premium (about 80% per older estimates).
pools.money_flow: Buyers and refinancers pay lender's and owner's policy premiums plus settlement fees at closing; independent agents retain most of the premium and underwriters keep the remainder and pay claims. Rates are state-filed, so there is no price competition.
pools.shock: Weak shock: Fannie Mae's title-waiver pilot lets certain refinances (LTV under 80%) skip the lender's title policy and attorney opinion letter using automated title review. Launched Nov 2024 with Doma, second vendor Westcor added July 2025, FHFA's Pulte wants it expanded, pilot end date Nov 30, 2027. KBW says refis are under 10% of title revenue so the earnings effect is small; ALTA says fraud/forgery is about 40% of refinance claim costs. Premiums are actually rising. I could not confirm any 2026 expansion to purchases (about 75% of mortgage volume), which is the real prize.
pools.incumbents: Underwriters 2025 share: First American 23.1%, Fidelity National 14.5%, Old Republic 14.0%, Chicago Title 13.1% (an FNF brand), Stewart 10.9%; thousands of independent agents do the local search/exam/closing work.
pools.incumbent_fragility: Revenue is priced as a percentage of loan or sale price while the work is a records search and an exam, so a waiver is a direct price attack. Counter: strong lobbying (ALTA, bipartisan legislators), fraud-claim data, and healthy margins mean incumbents are not under financial pressure.
pools.funded_startups_already_here: Qualia (closing software), Spruce, Snapdocs-type e-closing; Doma (first Fannie waiver vendor; I recall its 2024 sale to Title Resources Guaranty, from memory, not re-verified); Endpoint is a First American subsidiary after about $70M of investment (2020). My searches surfaced only 2018-2020 rounds and no 2023-26 venture rounds, a sign of a hard-to-disrupt, incumbent-friendly market.
pools.wedge_hints: Title-risk scoring data asset for lenders weighing waivers (path to a third waiver vendor with an insurance-backed product, like Westcor); automated county-record search and exam for agents; wire-fraud and closing-fund controls; curative (defect-fixing) outsourcing; payoff and lien verification.
pools.insider_roles: Title agency owners and escrow officers; underwriting counsel; title plant operators; lender secondary-market and QC staff; Fannie/Freddie title policy staff; title claims examiners.

pools.name: Creditors' contingency fees to US third-party debt collection agencies (medical, card, student and other defaulted debt)
pools.size_basis: First Research (Nov 2025): about 3,900 establishments, about $15B combined revenue, top 50 hold about half. A 2026 roundup citing IBISWorld says $21.4B across about 7,000 agencies, which I could not verify. Debt-buyer income (Encore, PRA) and creditors' in-house collection costs are on top. Used the conservative $15B.
pools.money_flow: Creditors (hospitals and physician groups, card issuers, telecoms, utilities, lenders) pay agencies roughly 20-40% of recoveries on contingency; debt buyers purchase defaulted paper at cents on the dollar.
pools.shock: Medical debt is 68.9% of furnished collections by contingency collectors (CFPB, 2018-2022). The CFPB rule to remove about $49B of medical debt from credit reports was finalized Jan 2025 then vacated July 2025; about 15 states now restrict medical-debt credit reporting (one mid-2026 blog count, verify with NCLC; Oregon SB 605 effective 2026-01-01) and at least 8 states considered limits on medical-debt wage garnishment in 2026. Federal student loans: collections restarted May 2025 but wage garnishment and Treasury offset were paused 2026-01-16 with no end date (about 5.3M borrowers in default). CFPB debt-collection complaints nearly doubled to about 207,800 in 2024. Net: the credit-report leverage that makes medical collections work is eroding state by state.
pools.incumbents: Debt buyers and agencies (Encore Capital, PRA Group, Conduent, Performant, Alorica, healthcare revenue-cycle firms; names from memory), with the 50 largest holding about half of revenue. The number of contingency-fee collectors fell 18% (815 to 672) from 2018 to 2022.
pools.incumbent_fragility: Call-center and letter workflows are expensive to adapt to 50 sets of state rules and to bans on credit reporting; the federal backstop (CFPB) is weakened, so the rules are a state patchwork. Counter: scale players have compliance staff and creditor relationships.
pools.funded_startups_already_here: From memory, rounds not re-verified: TrueAccord (digital-first collections), Symend (behavioral collections), Collectly (healthcare patient payments). No dedicated funding search was run for this pool.
pools.wedge_hints: Hospital-side product converting medical balances into payment plans or financing before collections, aimed at states with reporting bans; state-law rules engine (licensing, call limits, reporting bans, garnishment limits) licensed to agencies and small creditors; chain-of-title/documentation for debt-buyer portfolios ('debts I don't owe' is 45% of complaints); deceased-account and bankruptcy handling (overlaps with estate settlement); skip tracing and contact-consent management.
pools.insider_roles: Collection-agency compliance officers; hospital patient-financial-services directors; debt-buyer portfolio managers; FDCPA defense attorneys; state licensing specialists; student-loan guaranty-agency staff.

pools.name: US and Canadian financial institutions' financial-crime compliance operations (AML, KYC, sanctions screening, fraud)
pools.size_basis: Forrester/LexisNexis Risk Solutions survey (Feb 2024): US and Canada total cost of financial crime compliance $61B; labor is the largest line; 99% of institutions reported rising costs. Survey base was 160 US/Canada respondents out of 1,181 global; vendor-commissioned, so treat as upper-ish. Not a US-only number.
pools.money_flow: Banks, credit unions, broker-dealers, fintechs and money-service businesses pay in-house analysts, offshore operations centers, and software and data vendors for AML/KYC/sanctions/fraud work.
pools.shock: FinCEN's April 7, 2026 proposal replaces the 2024 proposal: defines an 'effective' AML/CFT program for the first time, shifts effort from low-risk to high-risk customers, reserves enforcement for systemic failures, standardizes four pillars (internal controls, independent testing, US-based compliance officer, training); comments closed June 9, 2026, effective 12 months after the final rule; FDIC/OCC/NCUA issued a companion bank proposal (Fed did not join). The investment-adviser AML rule was delayed to Jan 1, 2028. GENIUS Act adds AML duties for stablecoin issuers from Jan 2027. Mayer Brown reads the structure of obligations as largely unchanged, so the shock is how spend is allocated and examined, not a big cut.
pools.incumbents: Per-alert and per-seat vendors (NICE Actimize, Oracle, SAS, Fenergo, LexisNexis, Nasdaq Verafin; names from memory) plus BPO/offshore labor.
pools.incumbent_fragility: Effectiveness-based exams threaten alert-volume pricing because fewer alerts are acceptable if risk is covered; no FinCEN cost estimate was in the proposal summaries I read, and the final rule has not been confirmed.
pools.funded_startups_already_here: Sardine ($70M Series C Feb 2025, $660M valuation per third-party profile), Greenlite ($15M Series A May 2025, Greylock), Flagright ($12.5M Series A, undated), Castellum.AI ($8.5M Series A, undated), AiPrise ($12.5M Series A, undated), Diligent AI ($2.5M, March 2026), Marble (EUR 6.5M Series A, Sept 2026), Unit21 (latest round I saw was 2022). Hawk AI, Alloy, Parcha, Feedzai not verified this session.
pools.wedge_hints: Not copilots: (1) independent testing and 'effectiveness' validation for $1-5B banks, since the proposal makes independent testing a named pillar; (2) US-based BSA officer-as-a-service for fintech sponsors and foreign-owned US entities; (3) investment-adviser AML program build-out ahead of the 2028 date (about 15,000 RIAs, from memory); (4) sponsor-bank oversight for BaaS programs.
pools.insider_roles: BSA/AML officers at $1-5B community banks; former OCC and FDIC BSA examiners; SAR QA leads at offshore centers; sponsor-bank compliance heads; AML consultants and independent testers.

pools.name: Businesses' cross-border B2B payment fees and FX spread (stablecoin disruption after the GENIUS Act)
pools.size_basis: About $193B a year of international payments revenue, about 80% B2B, from a 2024 Visual Capitalist chart citing McKinsey (I did not find the 2025-report figure). McKinsey 2025: total payments revenue about $2.5T. For scale, one third-party estimate puts real stablecoin payment volume at about $390B a year (B2B about $226B), tiny against the pool.
pools.money_flow: Businesses pay banks, FX providers, correspondent networks and payment firms fees plus FX spread to send money across borders; fees are highest on small-ticket and emerging-market corridors.
pools.shock: GENIUS Act became law July 18, 2025. Agencies missed the July 2026 rulemaking deadline; the OCC said on 2026-08-19 it aims to finalize by November; effective date expected Jan 18, 2027 (draft rules: $5M capital floor, 10% same-day redeemability). Stablecoin market cap $317B on 2026-04-06 (Fed, secondary). Networks are buying in: Mastercard agreed to acquire BVNK for up to $1.8B (March 2026).
pools.incumbents: Correspondent banks, SWIFT, Wise, Payoneer, Airwallex, card networks, Circle, Ripple.
pools.incumbent_fragility: High fees on long-tail corridors are exposed to cheaper rails, but the networks are acquiring the winners (BVNK) rather than being displaced, so the rail itself is commoditizing and value moves to balance sheet, licenses and distribution.
pools.funded_startups_already_here: BVNK (Mastercard deal up to $1.8B after Coinbase's roughly $2B talks collapsed), Bridge (bought by Stripe for $1.1B; announced Oct 2024, my recollection is it closed early 2025 though one search summary implied Feb 2026), Zerohash (independent, reportedly raising $250M at $1.5B), Rain ($250M Series C Jan 2026), Noah ($38M seed Oct 2026), Cybrid ($10M Series A), Kast, Arq, Levl, VelaFi, Almond, Mesta.
pools.wedge_hints: All narrow, and most are dead ends without a lending balance sheet: corridor-specific working capital/trade finance for SMB importers, AR and treasury reconciliation for businesses receiving stablecoins, contractor payroll into specific emerging markets, GENIUS comparable-regime compliance for foreign issuers.
pools.insider_roles: Treasury managers at importers/exporters; freight-forwarder finance staff; correspondent-banking operations heads; MSB compliance officers; regional-bank FX desks.

pools.name: Merchant and issuer cost of card disputes and chargebacks (Visa VAMP monitoring)
pools.size_basis: LOW CONFIDENCE: about $33.8B of global chargeback value in 2025 rising to $41.7B by 2028 (Chargeflow blog; not confirmed in Mastercard pages). Mastercard/Datos: about 261M chargebacks in 2025 projected to reach 324M by 2028, issuer processing cost $9.08-10.32 per dispute (about $2.4-2.7B for issuers). This is value reversed from merchants, not fees; the vendor-addressable part is the portion merchants recover or avoid.
pools.money_flow: Card-not-present merchants lose the sale value on chargebacks, pay dispute fees and now network program fees; issuers spend about $9-10 per dispute; representment vendors take a share of recoveries.
pools.shock: Visa's VAMP (effective 2025-04-01) merges fraud and dispute counts into one ratio. Sources conflict on dates; most consistent account: merchant 'Excessive' enforcement from Oct 1, 2025, merchant threshold cut from 2.2% to 1.5% on April 1, 2026, fees about $4-8 per flagged transaction, acquirers graded on portfolio ratios so they cut or reserve risky merchants. Confirm against Visa rules before relying on any number.
pools.incumbents: Chargebacks911, Kount (Equifax), Riskified, Signifyd, Forter, and PSPs' own dispute tools (names from memory).
pools.incumbent_fragility: Networks keep changing rules and evidence formats and mid-size merchants have no dedicated dispute staff; acquirers now carry portfolio-level penalties and must police merchants.
pools.funded_startups_already_here: Chargeflow ($25M Series A Nov 2025, about $46M total per CB Insights), Justt ($30M Series C Dec 2024, about $100M total, targeting profitability by 2027), Chargebacks911; overlapping fraud platforms.
pools.wedge_hints: VAMP-ratio early-warning and deflection for mid-size merchants and ISOs/PSPs (before the TC40/TC15 count); acquirer-side merchant monitoring tooling; evidence packages for subscription, travel and digital-goods merchants; performance-fee models.
pools.insider_roles: Risk managers at PSPs and ISOs; acquirer merchant-risk analysts; dispute-operations managers at subscription and travel merchants; network-rules consultants.

pools.name: US fees paid to outside tax preparers and small-business accountants (capacity squeeze plus PE and AI roll-ups)
pools.size_basis: IBISWorld 2025 tax-preparation services revenue about $14.5B (seen via a search summary; VerticaIQ shows about $9.4B). Top 8 firms hold almost 40%. The full small-business bookkeeping, payroll and accounting services pool is larger but I found no primary Census or BLS number, so this undercounts.
pools.money_flow: Individuals and small businesses pay CPAs, enrolled agents, chains (H&R Block) and software (TurboTax) for returns, bookkeeping and advisory.
pools.shock: Labor: first-time CPA exam takers fell from 48,004 (2016) to 32,188 (2021) (AICPA via secondary source), the 75% retirement-eligible figure is an AICPA estimate from about 2020, and 150-hour-rule alternatives took effect in Ohio, Virginia and Georgia on Jan 1, 2026, and Iowa and Utah on July 1, 2026. Capital: IFAC counts 1,052 PE-linked accounting transactions 2015-2025 and Capstone a record 194 deals in 2025. Government: IRS Direct File is unavailable for the 2026 season (296,531 returns in 2025); OBBBA added tips, overtime and senior deductions, and H&R Block expects complexity to push filers to assisted prep (its own claim).
pools.incumbents: H&R Block (about 9,000 offices), Intuit TurboTax, independent CPAs and enrolled agents, PE-backed roll-ups (Crete Professionals Alliance, Thrive-backed, over $300M revenue, planned $500M+ of acquisitions in mid-2025).
pools.incumbent_fragility: Highly fragmented sole-proprietor supply that is aging out with a shrinking pipeline; roll-ups are consolidating, but most acquisitions target small firms and the labor constraint binds them too.
pools.funded_startups_already_here: Basis ($100M Series B, Feb 2026, $1.15B valuation), Rillet ($100M Series C, Aug 2026, $1B valuation), Crete (AI roll-up), plus Pilot, Fieldguide and Juno-type AI tax tools (from memory). Bench collapsed Dec 2024 (from memory).
pools.wedge_hints: Not copilots: financing and brokerage for retiring solo-CPA practices (buyers use SBA 7(a) loans, a lending or marketplace path); seasonal and overflow prep capacity networks of enrolled agents; succession and client-transition services; multi-state small-business compliance.
pools.insider_roles: Solo and small-firm CPAs and enrolled agents; practice brokers; PE-platform deal teams; state CPA society executives; IRS practitioner-liaison contacts.

pools.name: US estate settlement fees (probate, trust administration, fiduciary tax) during the great wealth transfer
pools.size_basis: My derivation: IBISWorld US estate-lawyer revenue $18.2B (2026); I assumed 30-50% is administration (probate and trust administration) rather than planning, giving $5.5-9B, midpoint 7; corporate trustee/executor fees excluded. Large uncertainty, treat as a floor. Context: Cerulli projects $124T of transfers through 2048 ($105T to heirs), about $2.5T a year to heirs now, above $3T by 2030 and above $4T about 2036. Third-party 'estate administration services' reports range from $1.5B (North America) to $15.8B (global) and are low quality.
pools.money_flow: Heirs and estates pay probate/estate attorneys, corporate trustees and executors, CPAs for final and fiduciary returns, appraisers and other providers during a 12-18 month settlement; financial advisors compete to keep or win the inherited assets (Cerulli: more than 70% of heirs likely to change their parents' advisor).
pools.shock: Alix raised a $20M Series A in July 2025 (Acrew, with Charles Schwab and Edward Jones Ventures), showing custodians and advisors paying to own settlement; Empathy has raised about $162M including a $72M Series C and distributes through insurers and employers. From memory, not re-verified: OBBBA set the estate and gift exemption at $15M per person from 2026, indexed, which cuts estate-tax planning urgency for most families and shifts value to administration.
pools.incumbents: Fragmented solo and small-firm probate attorneys (hourly or percentage fees, county-court processes), bank trust departments, and advisors whose revenue leaves when heirs do.
pools.incumbent_fragility: Process is manual, document-heavy and different in every state; banks hold the deceased's accounts but typically offer no service to heirs. Counter: distribution is being locked up by the funded players and courts set the pace.
pools.funded_startups_already_here: Empathy (about $162M total, $72M Series C), Alix (about $30.65M total, $20M Series A July 2025), plus planning-side players Trust & Will and Wealth.com (from memory).
pools.wedge_hints: White-label settlement operations for credit unions and community banks that hold the deceased's accounts but offer heirs nothing; inheritance-advance lending to heirs during probate (balance-sheet path); probate real-estate sale and retitling; account-closure and asset-retitling automation across institutions; unclaimed-asset search for estates.
pools.insider_roles: Probate attorneys and paralegals; trust officers; advisors who track heir attrition; probate court clerks; funeral directors; bank deceased-accounts teams.

pools.name: US state governments' spend on Medicaid and SNAP administration (eligibility determination, enrollment and verification systems, outsourced operations)
pools.geography: US (50 states; counties administer SNAP in 10 states)
pools.size_basis: Medicaid FY2024 administrative spending $41.3B federal+state (MACPAC Exhibit 31, parsed from PDF: eligibility systems $9.9B, MMIS $5.9B, other 50%-match functions incl. eligibility workers $23.0B; excludes managed-care plan admin). SNAP admin ~ $13B/yr derived [my estimate]: USDA regulatory analysis puts federal-to-state shift at ~$16.9B over FY2027-31 (CSPI), and the shift is 25 points of total admin cost. Addressable core (eligibility systems + operations) probably $15-25B [my estimate].
pools.money_flow: Federal government and states split admin cost (50% baseline, 90% federal match for system build, 75% for operations); states/counties pay system integrators and operations vendors (Maximus, Conduent, Gainwell, Deloitte, GDIT) plus their own and county caseworkers.
pools.shock: H.R.1 (P.L. 119-21, signed 2025-07-04): Medicaid work-requirement verification for expansion adults from 2027-01-01 (CMS interim final rule issued 2026-06-01, effective 2026-07-31; data-first verification, 6-month or quarterly checks); SNAP federal admin share cut from 50% to 25% on 2026-10-01 (~$16.9B shifted to states FY27-31; Maryland alone +$57.5M/yr); only $200M federal Medicaid implementation grants vs. states' costs; SNAP benefit cost-share tied to error rates starts FY2028.
pools.incumbents: Maximus (named by CMS as one of 10 existing E&E vendors pledging support), Deloitte, Gainwell, Conduent, GDIT, Accenture; earn on large implementation builds plus long operations contracts. CMS-brokered vendor deals: fixed fees for upgrades, discounted licenses, free fraud monitoring (claimed $600M savings through 2028).
pools.incumbent_fragility: States run patchwork legacy eligibility systems that cannot pull cross-agency data; vendors are under Senate scrutiny (Wyden/Warren letters to Deloitte, Gainwell, Conduent, GDIT, Maximus) and forced to discount; states are budget-squeezed by the SNAP cost shift and want per-verification pricing. Counterpoint: Jan 2027 go-live is so tight that first-wave money flows to existing vendors; newcomer window is 2027-2029 re-procurements and the verification data layer. Open-source/nonprofit tooling (Nava/APHSA) and USDA grants are free substitutes.
pools.funded_startups_already_here: Fortuna Health ($18M, July 2025, Medicaid enrollment/recertification); Nava PBC / Nava Labs ($1.2M grant, open-source AI verification for SNAP/Medicaid with APHSA and Maryland); Code for America (nonprofit); Equifax The Work Number (incumbent income verification). USDA FY26 SNAP earnings-verification grants up to $38M. Propel, Truv, Pinwheel not verified this session. No venture-scale direct attacker found.
pools.wedge_hints: (1) Per-verification employment/income data-matching for state agencies against 6-month and quarterly cycles; (2) exemption-evidence and document-capture tooling for county caseworkers in county-run SNAP states; (3) managed-care plans (capitation reasons to retain members) as payer for re-verification help, subject to outreach/marketing rules; (4) SNAP payment-error reduction before the FY2028 benefit cost-share. Payer who signs: state Medicaid or SNAP director via MES/human-services IT procurement.
pools.insider_roles: State Medicaid eligibility directors; county SNAP directors; state E&E/MMIS integration leads; MES procurement officers; managed-care plan enrollment and retention heads; Maximus/Conduent contract and site managers; legal-aid benefits attorneys; APHSA staff.

pools.name: US federal agencies' spend on management advisory and professional support services (consultants and support contractors)
pools.geography: US federal government (shock concentrated on civilian agencies)
pools.size_basis: Bloomberg Government (Jan 2026, paywalled, secondary): FY2025 management-advisory obligations fell 19% to a five-year low, civilian down one-third to $26B and DoD down 1% to $24B. GAO FY2025 snapshot (total contract commitments ~$793B; professional support services ~$26B at DoD and ~$18B civilian, a narrower category).
pools.money_flow: Agencies pay labor-hour/time-and-materials fees to primes (Booz Allen, Deloitte GPS, Accenture Federal, SAIC, CACI, Leidos) and to small-business subcontractors via GSA schedules and IDIQs.
pools.shock: Feb 2025 GSA memo told agencies to review and justify contracts with the 10 highest-paid consulting firms (>$65B in fees in 2025 and later); Bloomberg reported ~1,700 GSA consulting terminations claiming $4.5B savings, then a second phase pushing outcome-based restructuring ($8.9B immediate savings claimed). Deloitte at least 127 contracts cut or modified, Booz Allen ~61, Accenture at least 30 ($240M).
pools.incumbents: Booz Allen (almost all of ~$11B revenue is public sector), Deloitte Government and Public Services, Accenture Federal (federal ~8% of global revenue FY2024), SAIC, CACI, Leidos; revenue depends on billable headcount.
pools.incumbent_fragility: Labor-hour model conflicts with outcome-based buying and AI productivity; civilian demand down by a third and agencies must defend spend. Counterpoint: DoD contract spend is growing ($491.6B FY2025 vs $445B), so the shock is civilian-only; moats are past performance, set-asides and clearances.
pools.funded_startups_already_here: No funded AI-native delivery firm selling services to federal civilian agencies found. Funded players are software for contractors: NationGraph ($18M Series A, Feb 2026), Vultron ($22M Series A, 2025), Ask Sage ($17M Series A, Dec 2024), Procurement Sciences AI ($10M Series A, 2024). Real competitors are mid-size GovCons with set-aside status; big firms repositioning toward agent delivery.
pools.wedge_hints: Fixed-price, outcome-priced work replacing terminated time-and-materials contracts at civilian agencies (claims backlogs, grants management, FOIA, IT modernization); subcontract slots with primes that must reprice; small-business set-aside entry (status of SBA 8(a)/set-aside programs in 2026 not verified, check). Payer who signs: contracting officer with agency CIO/program office as sponsor.

pools.name: US farm employers' H-2A guest-worker wage bill and the recruiter / farm-labor-contractor / compliance layer around it
pools.size_basis: FY2025 H-2A wage bill $6,935M (FY24: $6.5B) on ~398,000 certified positions, from UC Davis Rural Migration News built on DOL OFLC data. 44% of jobs certified to farm labor contractors (FLCs); 7 of top-10 H-2A employers are FLCs; agents filed 56% of applications; ~9,700 registered FLCs/employees (~4,000 active businesses, Mar 2026). Total US farm labor ~$53B/yr (Farm Bureau/ERS forecast). Service-fee layer (FLC markups, agent fees, housing, transport) is additional and not sized in sources. Path to $100M revenue needs ~15% of a ~$700M fee pool at 10%, i.e. heroic share, or a gross-billing employer-of-record model.
pools.money_flow: Growers pay AEWR-floor wages plus free housing, transport and visa costs. FLCs act as employer of record and bill growers wages plus markup. Agents recruit abroad (mostly Mexico) and file ETA-790 job orders and visa paperwork.
pools.shock: DOL interim final rule (published Oct 2, 2025) replaced the USDA-survey AEWR with a two-tier OEWS-based AEWR plus a $1-3/hr housing adjustment for H-2A workers only; mode AEWR fell from $17 to $14/hr in FY26 Q1; DOL projects >$2B/yr employer savings, EPI estimates $4.4-5.4B/yr lost wages. On Aug 26, 2026 the E.D. Cal. (UFW v. DOL) held the rule unlawful but declined to vacate, ordered DOL to produce a new methodology 'promptly' (no deadline) and to notify employers they may owe backpay. Wage regime is now legally unsettled with retroactive true-up risk.
pools.incumbents: ~4,000 active FLCs (half of H-2A jobs), foreign recruiting agents (56% of filings), regional grower associations, ag-labor law firms. Nobody owns payroll + housing + recruiting + compliance end to end.
pools.incumbent_fragility: Thousands of small FLCs/agents on paper-heavy compliance (ETA-790, housing inspections, wage records), thin working capital and joint-employer liability, and now a wage rate in legal limbo with possible backpay. Fragmentation prevents a coordinated response.
pools.funded_startups_already_here: Seso (SF): $25M Series A 2022 led by Index; $26M Series B 2024 led by Bond (Mary Meeker) with Index/NFX; H-2A compliance, payroll, HR, worker banking. Croft (Indianapolis, seed Feb 2024, ~$2.7M per Caplight). Yadag (Toronto, ~$0.8M per CB Insights). H2 Organizer (Austin, product launch Sep 2024). No 2025-26 round found, but only one search run.
pools.wedge_hints: Backpay-exposure modeling/escrow/insurance by job order; FLC back office (payroll, wage statements, worker banking); working-capital/factoring for FLCs who pay weekly and collect late; employer-provided housing at scale (modular or leaseback); monitoring foreign recruiters for banned worker-paid fees; H-2B (non-ag) adjacent program.
pools.insider_roles: FLC owners/operators; grower-association H-2A managers; ag-labor attorneys; farm HR/payroll managers; labor recruiters in Mexico; former DOL Wage and Hour investigators; farmworker-housing inspectors.

pools.size_basis: USDA ERS FY2024: four child-nutrition programs cost $28.2B for 9.3B meals; NSLP alone $17.7B (4.83B lunches; $16.15B cash + $1.56B commodities per FNS data); CRS puts federal child nutrition at ~$32B. State, local and student payments are additional.
pools.money_flow: USDA reimburses per meal and supplies commodities; student payments add; districts either self-operate or hire management companies, which buy from distributors and processors and employ kitchen labor.
pools.shock: California AB 1264 signed Oct 8, 2025 (first US statutory definition and phase-out of 'ultraprocessed foods of concern' in schools; regulations due Jun 1, 2028, district phase-out from Jul 1, 2029, vendor ban from 2032, though some sources say 2035). USDA added-sugar limits began SY2025-26 with a weekly limit in 2027-28; sodium cuts delayed to 2027-28; whole milk allowed again in 2026; USDA drafting a new meal-pattern rule. Operative dates are 2029+, so the why-now is real but slow.
pools.incumbents: Sodexo, Compass (Chartwells) and Aramark dominate the contracted segment; Cenavera (Nautic Partners investment, about Oct 2025, date unconfirmed; 350+ districts in 33 states); most districts self-operate.
pools.incumbent_fragility: Fixed federal reimbursement cannot cover scratch-cooking labor; kitchens were built to reheat; the definition of ultraprocessed foods of concern does not exist yet; ~13,000 small buyers.
pools.funded_startups_already_here: The Yay Company ($12M Series A Nov 2021, $15.5M total), Ordo (Series A Oct 2022), Revolution Foods (debt Oct 2023). No new venture rounds found for 2023-2026 (aggregator data, may be incomplete); recent capital is private equity (Cenavera).
